Global Reading Atlas¶

Reading, listening and genres in public survey data¶

A reproducible analytical companion to the dashboard. Evidence review: 25 October 2026. The requested evidence starts in 2022 and includes reviewed 2026 survey observations. Older US observations remain a labelled historical reference. This report measures published survey observations; the evidence supports a comparable European section and distinct national profiles.

tl;dr¶

  • 32 European countries have usable 2022 observations. Book participation ranges from 29.2% in Albania to 80.6% in Switzerland. The official EU aggregate is 52.8%. Eurostat includes audiobooks in this measure.
  • Women have higher reported participation in all 32 assessable countries. Higher education is also associated with higher participation within every assessable country; the median tertiary-minus-low-education gap is 38.6 percentage points. These subgroup patterns describe association.
  • US audiobook participation rose from 11% in 2011 to 23% in 2021 in the phone-survey period. The 26% result in 2025 uses a changed survey mode and is shown separately.
  • Canadian reported fiction genres vary by format: mysteries/thrillers lead the reported print, ebook and audiobook lists. History leads its separate nonfiction lists. Singapore adds a broader mixed-material genre view. The expanded coverage section adds other source-specific genre studies, including audiobook listener choices in Germany, France, Italy and Spain. Survey populations and questions remain separate.

Reading rule: percentages with different denominators or recall periods stay in separate views. No all-world participation estimate, causal model, or survey-design confidence interval is inferred.

Context & Methods¶

The central question is how book use differs by geography, format and demographic group, and what public surveys reveal about genres. The analysis has three distinct units:

Question Observation unit Scope
European participation Country × 2022 × population group Eurostat EU-SILC; age 16+
Format use Country × survey year × format × stated population Separate survey profiles
Genre preferences Country × source × question × format × genre × survey base National reading surveys and separate audiobook listener studies

Key Assumptions¶

  1. Eurostat participation is 100 − percentage reporting zero books; the source includes print, ebooks and audiobooks and excludes school textbooks and work manuals. It cannot identify listening separately from reading.
  2. Demographic gaps subtract percentages for the same country, year, age scope and education scope. Groups are never summed. An unweighted country median describes this observed country set; it is not a population-weighted European rate.
  3. Source flags matter: unreliable values (u) and missing observations remain missing. Published estimated values (e) remain identified. Germany is retained in data, excluded from numerical rankings, and never filled with zero.
  4. Format use and genre choices overlap. Genre percentages represent selecting a category within the reported survey base, not market share or the proportion of all books consumed.
  5. The source files contain aggregate survey tables. National respondent microdata, design weights and subgroup sample sizes are unavailable here. No valid design-based uncertainty, significance test or individual-level effect can be calculated from these tables.

Results¶

4. European participation in 2022¶

This is the strongest geographically comparable section: the same Eurostat table, survey year, baseline age and format definition. Countries are ordered by published point estimates; uncertainty is unavailable, so this is not a significance ranking. The displayed geography includes EU members and other countries covered by the survey. The dashed reference is the official EU27 aggregate.

Observed spread: Switzerland 80.6% versus Albania 29.2%, a 51.4 percentage point difference. The observed set contains 26 EU members and 6 other surveyed countries. The unweighted country median is 53.4%; it is distinct from the official EU aggregate of 52.8%.

5. The gender pattern within countries¶

This comparison fixes country, year, age 16+ and all education levels. The reported source categories are women and men. Differences are percentage points, with no causal interpretation or statistical significance claim.

Women have higher reported participation in 32/32 assessable countries. The unweighted median gap is 15.9 percentage points, with country gaps from 3.6 to 30.7 points.

6. Age profiles within countries¶

Four non-overlapping age bands are shown independently. Each cell uses its own age-group denominator. The heatmap follows overall participation order for lookup; its cells are never combined into an unweighted overall rate. Darker cells mean higher participation.

The 16–29 rate exceeds the 65+ rate in 28/32 assessable countries. The median within-country difference is 9.5 percentage points. These age comparisons also reflect cohort and population composition.

7. Exploratory statistics: is the education pattern sensitive to age scope?¶

A small paired analysis compares tertiary education (ISCED 5–8) with primary/lower-secondary education or below (ISCED 0–2) in each country. We repeat the subtraction among people aged 30–54, rather than fitting an unsupported individual-level predictive model.

This narrows the age range but is not an age-standardised or causal effect. The two scopes overlap, so they are compared as a sensitivity check and never pooled as independent observations. Descriptive medians and rank correlation summarise the observed countries; p-values and confidence intervals are omitted because countries are not a random survey sample and source survey design information is unavailable.

Country set Countries Median gap, age 16+ (pp) Median gap, age 30–54 (pp) Positive in both scopes
All observed countries 32 38.6 48.1 32
Observed EU members only 26 37.5 48.1 26

Descriptive rank agreement: Spearman ρ = 0.81. Leaving out one country at a time gives 0.79–0.85. This sensitivity range is not a confidence interval.

The education gap is positive in all 32 countries in both scopes. The median is 38.6 points for age 16+ and 48.1 points for age 30–54. The direction persists when the age scope narrows, but the gap size changes.

8. US formats: an observed trend and a survey-method break¶

Pew reports at least part of one book in each format during the previous 12 months among US adults aged 18+. Respondents can use multiple formats. Survey years are irregular and are plotted at their actual calendar positions. The 2025 mode changed from phone to a combination of web and phone; its result is separated from the phone-period line.

Audiobook participation increased 12 percentage points from 2011 (11%) to 2021 (23%). The 2025 observation is 26%; a 2021-to-2025 change mixes behaviour and possible survey-mode effects.

9. National format profiles, with their own denominators¶

Each panel is a separate reading question. Canada is an English-speaking online reader sample; Singapore is the subset able to remember at least one book; Sweden and Norway measure average-day reach; the US measures annual participation among adults. These panels show local format patterns. Their heights do not establish a valid cross-country ranking.

10. Canadian fiction genres by format¶

BookNet Canada's 2024 survey uses an unweighted English-speaking adult online panel with a recruited reader base. This genre question concerns fiction readers within each format, with up to three selections. Exact format-fiction subgroup sample sizes are unpublished in the extracted table. The published dash for audiobook comics/graphic novels is missing, not zero. Labels below retain the source's categories, including “Chick Lit”.

Format Leading reported genre Selected (%)
Audiobook Mysteries or Thrillers 46
Ebook Mysteries or Thrillers 44
Print Mysteries or Thrillers 56

The same genre leads all three reported format lists. Format-specific differences may reflect different reader populations, preferences and survey routing; they are not an effect of converting a book to audio.

11. Canadian non-fiction subjects by format¶

This is a separate BookNet question and reader base: non-fiction readers within each format. We retain all ten published subjects and the missing audiobook comics/graphic-novel entry. Subject choices can overlap, and exact subgroup sample sizes are unpublished. Fiction and non-fiction percentages are not added or treated as sharing the same denominator.

Format Leading reported subject Selected (%)
Audiobook History 34
Ebook History 33
Print History 39

History leads the reported non-fiction lists at 39% for print, 33% for ebooks and 34% for audiobooks. This pattern describes the recruited format-specific readers, rather than all Canadian adults or sales demand.

12. Singapore: a broader genre question¶

NLB's 2024 genre question concerns general readers (n=3,657), citizens or permanent residents aged 20+. It includes websites, social media, books, ebooks and magazines, with a “usually” recall frame. Its reported genres help describe the local reading environment; they cannot be placed on the Canadian book-fiction scale or treated as audiobook genre preferences.

Humorous stories (42%) leads this six-category published view. This is a separate question and denominator from Singapore's format-use subset of n=2,693.

Select one country, source and genre question¶

The parameters above select a single reviewed country, survey source, question, format and observation year. The default uses Germany's 2025 audiobook listener study commissioned by Audible and conducted by Verian. It complements the Canadian format questions and the separate 2026 Story Report. The full country survey had 1,000 online respondents aged 18 to 65; the exact audiobook listener subset size is unpublished. No broader podcast audience is used here.

Question: Audiobook genres among past-year listeners. Recall: past_12_months_listener_base. Population: Online respondents aged 18 to 65; country survey n=1000; commissioned by Audible and conducted by Verian. Original source. Locator: Infographics PDF p.2, Die beliebtesten Hörbuch-Genres in Deutschland, Frankreich, Italien und Spanien, Germany panel; respondent base and multiple-answer footnote.

Only five published categories per country. Multiple answers allowed, not market shares. Fieldwork July 2025, publication 13 October 2025. Original category labels retained from German-language infographic. This is audiobook listener genre choice, not national audiobook participation. Do not reuse the separate combined audiobook/audio-drama/podcast audience headline.

Categories may overlap. A reported top five omits other choices; absence is not zero. These percentages describe this survey base and do not establish national listening participation or catalogue market shares.

Published book industry evidence¶

Monetary evidence is separate from reader participation. The same industry table used in the dashboard and audiobook notebook covers publisher receipts, retail turnover, operating revenue and source-defined sales estimates. Its country profiles retain their own currency and scope. Some countries have only a historical 2022 observation; unpublished years remain missing. Detailed measures, original source links and report vintages are in industry_metrics.csv.

Takeaways¶

  1. Use Europe for country comparisons of total book participation. Keep the 2022 survey year and inclusion of audio visible. The results describe participation, rather than reading volume, sales, literacy or current behaviour.
  2. Use within-country demographics for segmentation hypotheses. The education direction persists in a narrower age band, but gaps remain unadjusted. Testing causes would require microdata, survey design information and a defensible research design.
  3. Use US history for format adoption during a consistent survey regime. Treat 2025 as its own mode period. More audiobooks and more ebooks can coexist with print because users overlap.
  4. Use national format and genre panels for source-specific profiles. The expanded inventory includes annual, weekly and reader-subset listening plus different genre questions. Its bases limit generalisation. Genre mappings should preserve original labels before any future harmonisation.
  5. Expand coverage by comparable source families. The worldwide source register is a discovery framework, not evidence that every country has comparable observations. Add original survey tables and complete the definition/denominator checks before extending rankings.

The next defensible research step is to add national annual format surveys with matching adult populations and recall periods, then obtain accessible microdata or published design-based intervals for uncertainty. Predictive modelling should wait for a larger comparable dataset.
